parts.title: How Many Mesopredators Live in Hungary, and Where Do They Live? Counting Burrows and Watching Wildlife Cameras
parts.abstract:
In Central Europe, medium-sized predators such as badgers, foxes and jackals are becoming more common. To manage hunting and wildlife well, we need to keep a careful eye on them. In this study, we set out to estimate the smallest possible number of European badgers (Meles meles), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) and golden jackals (Canis aureus), and how many young they produce. We worked in two hunting areas in southwestern Hungary, called Drávaszentes and Darány.

First, in early 2025, we counted every burrow in each area. Then we placed wildlife cameras at burrows that animals were using, to record adults and their young, called cubs. In Drávaszentes, we found 1.05 occupied badger burrows and 0.38 occupied fox burrows for every 100 hectares of land. (A hectare is a square 100 metres on each side.) The average litter, meaning the young born together in one go, held 1.13 cubs for badgers and 2.33 cubs for foxes. In Darány, there were 1.43 occupied badger burrows per 100 hectares, and golden jackals were present at 0.2 per 100 hectares.

We also looked at which kinds of land the animals preferred. Using a mapping program called QGIS, we drew a circle with a 400-metre radius around each burrow. We then compared the land types inside these circles with the land types around randomly chosen points. The results suggested that, in each area, the animals preferred certain kinds of land: farmland that is not watered by irrigation, and mixed forests. These findings give a starting point for understanding how predator numbers change over time, so that people can make well-informed decisions about managing them.
parts.introduction_first:
In places where the very largest predators, such as wolves, have been pushed out or kept down, scientists are paying more and more attention to medium-sized predators. These are called mesopredators. When the top hunters disappear, the food chain gets shorter, and medium-sized predators often move up to eat animals they would not have eaten before [1,2]. That is why studying them helps us understand how nature works [3].

An idea called the mesopredator release theory says that as the number of medium-sized predators grows, they put more pressure on the animals they hunt. This effect, which works from the top of the food chain downward, can also change how many different kinds of living things an area holds [1].

Medium-sized predators also matter for money. This is true for people who protect nature and for people who manage hunting. In several ways, these predators cost money. For example, they kill animals that are protected by law, as well as small game animals that hunters shoot. On top of that, controlling predators can be expensive, because it takes traps, guns and a lot of time.
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

Our first hypothesis was that most occupied burrows would be used by red foxes. Our data did not support it. Badgers had the most burrows, so we conclude that badgers have the largest population in the areas we studied. Across Hungary as a whole, the estimated number of red foxes is twice the number of badgers [4]. In our local areas, though, there could be fewer foxes. Badgers may have an advantage over foxes because they are bigger and live in groups [38].

Our second hypothesis was that litter sizes would be about the same as in earlier studies. We rejected it. Badger litters had between 1 and 2 cubs, which matches what other researchers have published [7]. Red fox litters, however, had between 1 and 3 cubs, which is smaller than earlier studies found [38]. Small or shrinking litters could be a sign that the land is poor for the animals, especially if there is not enough food [39]. For golden jackals, we found too few occupied burrows (only 2) to draw any conclusions.

Our third hypothesis was that the kinds of land around burrows would differ between burrows with cubs and burrows without cubs. Our data did not support it either. When we compared the area of each land type around burrows with cubs and around randomly chosen points, we found only a few differences. In the other cases, the land was the same. Future studies should look more closely at the small-scale surroundings of burrows [39], using more burrows and a more detailed analysis.
parts.introduction_rest:
In a large part of Central Europe, including Hungary, three animals are seen as widespread medium-sized predators: the red fox (Vulpes vulpes Linnaeus, 1758), the Eurasian badger (Meles meles Linnaeus, 1758) and the golden jackal (Canis aureus Linnaeus, 1758). The red fox was the predator with the most individuals in Hungary in the 2000s and 2010s [4]. The European badger was added to the list of animals that people may hunt in 2001, because it lives all over the country [5,6].

The golden jackal has a more dramatic story. In the 1980s, Hungary was one of the first countries where the species came back to Europe [7,8]. Between 1940 and 1990, no jackals were recorded breeding, so the species was declared extinct in 1989 [9]. In the early 1990s, jackals began to return, and their numbers grew so fast that they became a species that people may hunt in 1994. From then until 1999, and again from 2012 onwards, they could be hunted at any time of year. In the years in between, the hunting season ran from 1 July to the end of February [10,11].

Medium-sized predators do more than hunt other animals and compete with them. Foxes and badgers are also known to spread diseases that can harm the health of both animals and people [12]. All of this makes it important to manage predators carefully, based on real measurements. To do that, we need to understand how their numbers change over time and which places they choose to live in [13,14].

Foxes and badgers live in burrows, so it helps to know where these underground shelters are. However, counting burrows to estimate how many animals there are can be thrown off by the way the animals behave. For example, badgers can live alone or in groups called clans [15]. Foxes, on the other hand, may use several burrows over a period of time, which can make the population seem larger than it really is [16]. Foxes and badgers may also share the same burrows, and some burrow entrances may be used only in certain seasons [17]. Golden jackals can use burrows too, but most of the time they shelter on the ground surface [18].

The mix of these animals also differs from region to region, depending on the kind of natural habitat in each area [19,20]. For all these reasons, it is important to keep watch on the burrows we find and to use what we learn to help manage predators.

### Our hypotheses

We carried out our study in two hunting areas in southwestern Hungary that are managed in different ways. One is a nature conservation area. There, the main goal is to protect the variety of living things and to keep natural processes going, and hunting is strictly controlled. Any work that changes the land must be kept to a minimum and done with great care. The other area focuses on wildlife management. There, the main goal is to make sure the land can be used in a way that can last, and hunting is the main tool for reaching that goal.

With this in mind, our study had two main aims: (1) to use wildlife cameras to estimate the smallest possible number of foxes, badgers and jackals per burrow; and (2) to describe the kinds of land around the burrows that animals were using. Based on these aims, we made the following hypotheses:

Most occupied burrows are used by red foxes.

The litter sizes we see in these predators will be about the same as those reported in earlier studies from Hungary.

The kinds of land around a burrow have a statistically significant effect on how it is used. (A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.) We expect this effect to differ between burrows with cubs, burrows without cubs, and randomly chosen points.
parts.methods:
2. What We Studied and How

2.1. Where We Worked

Our first study area, Drávaszentes, lies in the southern part of Somogy County, between the towns of Barcs, Komlósd and Péterhida (coordinates: 45.997562561, 17.396221579). It is a special hunting area managed by the Danube-Drava National Park Directorate. The whole area covers 1138 hectares, and 1042 hectares of it are used for hunting.

Drávaszentes sits in the Middle Drava Valley, a small local region. It lies on a high floodplain, which is flat land beside a river that floods from time to time, and it sits in the old bed of the Drava River. Because of this, the area is 10–20 m lower than the land around it, and only its eastern side is hilly. Most of it is flat plain, with heights differing by only a few metres. The lowest point is 94 m above sea level and the highest is 130 m.

The climate is moderately humid. The average temperature over a year is 10.0–10.2 °C, and about 780–800 mm of rain and snow falls each year. Two small streams run through the area, the Györgyös stream and the Komlósdi-Rinya. They also meet inside the area, but both dry up in drier years. The groundwater, the water held in the soil and rock underground, lies close to the surface. It can be found everywhere, at a depth of about 2–4 m [21].

To find out which kinds of land the area has, we used the mapping program QGIS (version 3.30.1) with a map layer called Corine Land Cover. This layer sorts land into types, each given a code. The most common land type was broad-leaved forest (code 311), which covered 46% of the area. Pastures (code 231) were also very common, covering 34.2%. Next came farmland that is not watered by irrigation (code 211), at 14.9%. Smaller shares were built-up areas with scattered buildings (code 112), at 3.6%, and farmland with a lot of natural plants growing on it (code 243), at 1.3% (Figure 1).

Our second study area, Darány, is also in the southern part of Somogy County, between the towns of Barcs and Darány (coordinates: 45.986786021, 17.533621622). It covers 980.8 hectares and lies in the Eastern-Inner Somogy region. The land is flat, with the lowest point at 125 m above sea level and the highest at 145 m. The climate is moderately humid, with an average yearly temperature of 10.0 to 10.3 °C, and more than 800 mm of rain and snow falls each year.

The Rigóc stream runs through Darány, but it dries out in drier years. The area also has 9 fishponds. Only 5 of them hold water, and in the dry season all of them dry out except 2. The rest are covered in reeds and bushes. The groundwater lies between 2 and 4 m deep [21].

We worked out the land types in Darány in the same way as for Drávaszentes. Here, broad-leaved forest (code 311) covered the most land, at 42.4%, followed closely by mixed forest (code 313), at 40.6%. Farmland that is not watered by irrigation (code 211) covered 9.8% of the area, and water bodies (code 512) covered 5.1%. Coniferous forest (code 312) covered 1.9%, and land where shrubs are slowly turning into woodland (code 324) covered 0.2% (Figure 2).

2.2. How We Collected Our Data

2.2.1. Counting Burrows in the Field

To find the burrows, we counted every burrow in both study areas. This gave us the most reliable data we could. We did this counting in 2025, from February to April. Early spring is the best time to see burrows, because the plants have not yet grown thick enough to hide them.

Throughout the fieldwork, we recorded every burrow we found on maps and with a handheld GPS device (Garmin GPSmap 62s, made in Olathe, Kansas, USA). We recorded positions using Hungary's national map system, called the Unified National Projection System (EOV).

We counted a hole as a burrow if it was deeper than one metre and big enough for the body of the animal we were studying [22]. The entrance was usually between 15 and 60 cm wide, which is a good size for a badger or a red fox to shelter in [23] (Figure A1, Figure A2 and Figure A3). When the nearest entrances were more than 50 m apart, we counted them as separate burrows [22].

We kept a field log with the GPS position of each burrow. The log also gave each burrow a number, noted whether it was occupied, and recorded which species used it. We told which species was using a burrow by looking for tracks, footprints, scent marks, droppings and latrines (places where animals leave their droppings) [22]. We counted a burrow as occupied if its entrances looked clean and showed signs of recent activity. Badgers leave their own typical signs, which helped us tell their burrows apart from those of other species [24,25,26,27,28].

2.2.2. Counting the Fewest Animals and the Number of Cubs with Wildlife Cameras

Where we could, we placed wildlife cameras at burrows that animals were using. These cameras take a picture when an animal moves in front of them, and they let us record the smallest possible number of adults and young living in each burrow. Camera traps are very useful for animals that are active at night or that are hard to spot [29]. From the photos, we found the largest number of cubs and adults seen together at one time at each burrow.

We used 6 cameras that could send their pictures to us and 15 cameras that could not. We set the cameras to take a photo 3 seconds after sensing movement, and we switched off the setting that takes several photos in a row. We set the picture quality to 5 megapixels and the motion sensor (a passive infrared sensor, or PIR, which notices the heat of a moving animal) to its normal setting.

We climbed a ladder to put each camera on a nearby tree, about 2.5 m up and about 5 m from the entrance that animals were using. We fixed the cameras to the tree with Python (QGIS Desktop 3.30.1) cables. In Drávaszentes, we watched the burrows from 18 April 2025 to 6 May 2025, which is 16 days. In Darány, we watched them from 20 May 2025 to 8 June 2025, which is 19 days. Some burrows had several entrances, and at these we placed cameras at different entrances. The cameras we used were made by Bushnell (Nature View), Reconyx (HC500), Uovison (Easy Mail, Select 30, 565) and Minox (DTC 400, DTC 650).

At large burrows with several entrances, we could not always place a camera at the entrance that the predators used. This probably meant we could not always count the adults and young exactly. In open grassland, there was also a higher risk that people without permission would take the cameras, so we used fewer cameras there. In these cases, we worked out the smallest possible number of animals from the tracks we saw. Altogether, we watched 31 burrows with cameras: 15 in Drávaszentes and 16 in Darány.

2.2.3. Working Out Which Kinds of Land Badgers Live Around

To find out which kinds of land surround the burrows that animals were using, we drew a circle with a 400-metre radius around each of these burrows. We did this with the mapping program Quantum GIS 3.31.1 and a land map layer called Corine Land Cover 100 (version 2018) [30]. First, we laid the land map over the circles. This showed us how much of each land type fell inside each circle [31].

Next, we placed random points in the study areas, five times over. The number of random points was the same as the number of occupied burrows in each study area. For the random points, we also worked out the land types inside a circle with a 400-metre radius. We had enough occupied burrows for this kind of comparison only for badgers.

2.3. How We Analysed the Data

2.3.1. Looking at the Wildlife Camera Photos

We went through all the camera photos and sorted them into separate folders, one folder for each burrow. The photos let us count how many adults lived in each burrow, and from this we worked out the size of the population each year. We also counted the cubs. This let us work out the average number of cubs in the burrows, and the number of cubs in all the occupied burrows together. Adding the adults and the cubs together gave us the smallest possible number of animals living in the area.

2.3.2. Comparing the Land Around Burrows with and without Cubs

For the statistics, we split the occupied burrows into two groups: burrows with cubs and burrows without cubs. We then used a test called the Mann–Whitney U-test. This test checks whether the values in one group tend to be higher or lower than in another group. We used it to compare the area of each land type around burrows with cubs with the area of the same land types around burrows without cubs and around the random points. We did these calculations in Microsoft Excel and in the statistics program GraphPad Instat 3.
parts.results:
3. Results

3.1. How Many Burrows There Were

3.1.1. Drávaszentes

In the Drávaszentes study area, we found 23 burrows. Fifteen belonged to badgers and 7 to foxes (Figure 1). Of the 15 badger burrows, 11 were occupied, and of the 7 fox burrows, 4 were occupied. Two of these occupied burrows were used by both species.

From these counts, we worked out that there were 1.05 occupied badger burrows and 0.38 occupied fox burrows for every 100 hectares of land.

We also measured how far apart the burrows were. The closest two badger burrows were 627 m apart, and the farthest were 5407 m apart, with an average of 2524 m. For foxes, the closest two burrows were 1346 m apart and the farthest were 4173 m apart, with an average of 2722 m. The nearest fox burrow to a badger burrow was 303 m away.

3.1.2. Darány

In the Darány study area, we found 42 burrows. Of these, 24 belonged to badgers and 18 to members of the dog family, the canids (Figure 2). The 24 badger burrows were occupied, and so were 14 of them. Among the canid burrows, none of the 16 fox burrows were occupied, but both of the 2 golden jackal burrows were.

This gives 1.43 occupied badger burrows, 0 occupied fox burrows and 0.2 occupied golden jackal burrows for every 100 hectares of land.

The closest two badger burrows were 186 m apart, and the farthest were 3757 m apart, with an average of 1722 m. The two jackal burrows we found were 2231 m apart. The nearest jackal burrow to a badger burrow was 407 m away.

3.2. How Many Animals We Estimated per Burrow from Wildlife Cameras

3.2.1. Drávaszentes

Our wildlife cameras recorded at least the following numbers of animals in the 11 badger burrows we watched. We saw cubs in eight of these burrows: one cub in seven burrows and two cubs in one. From this, we worked out an average of 1.13 cubs per burrow. Spread across all the occupied burrows, that comes to 0.82 cubs per burrow. We never saw a litter with more than two cubs, and in total we counted nine cubs.

We also saw 15 adults in the occupied burrows, which works out to 1.36 adults per burrow. Adding adults and cubs together gives 2.18 animals per burrow. So we estimate that at least 24 badgers live in this area, and 15 of them are the core population, meaning the animals that live in the area all year round.

The cameras also recorded at least the following numbers of animals in the four fox burrows we watched. We saw fox cubs in three of them: one cub in one burrow and three cubs in two burrows. This gives an average of 2.33 cubs per burrow in the burrows that had cubs, and 1.75 cubs per burrow across all the occupied burrows. We saw 1.25 adults per burrow. Altogether we recorded seven cubs. Adding the 5 adults and the cubs together gives three animals per burrow. So we estimate that at least 13 foxes live in this area, and 5 of them are the core population.

3.2.2. Darány

Our wildlife cameras recorded at least the following numbers of animals in the 14 badger burrows we watched. Here we saw cubs on five occasions: one cub in two burrows and two cubs in three burrows. This gives an average of 1.6 cubs per burrow. Spread across all the occupied burrows, that comes to 0.58 cubs per burrow. We never saw a litter with more than two cubs, and in total we counted eight cubs.

We saw 1.57 adults per burrow. Adding adults and cubs together gives 2.15 animals per burrow. So we estimate that at least 30 badgers live in this area, and 22 of them are the core population.

At the two jackal burrows we watched, the cameras recorded only adults (2 cases). That gives 1 adult per burrow. So we estimate that at least two golden jackals live in this area, and both are part of the core population.

3.3. Which Kinds of Land Badger Burrows Were Near

3.3.1. Drávaszentes

In Drávaszentes, we compared the land around burrows with cubs to the land around randomly chosen points. We looked at six groups of points: one group of 5 points, which we call "random 5", and five groups of 1 point, which we call "random 1" to "random 5". We looked at five land types.

For one land type, farmland that is not watered by irrigation (called CLC 211 in the land maps), we found a statistically significant difference between burrows with cubs and the "random 5" points (Table A1). A difference is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. Here, "rarely" means less than 5% of the time.

The middle value, or median, tells the same story. Around burrows with cubs, the median area of this farmland was 18.42 hectares, much higher than the 0.64 hectares around the "random 5" points (Table A3). This might mean that, in this area, badgers more often dig their breeding burrows in places where a large share of the land within 400 m is this kind of farmland.

For the other land types, we could not find a statistically significant difference (p > 0.05), or we could not run the test because we did not have enough data. These land types were broad-leaved forest (CLC 311), built-up areas that are broken up into separate patches (CLC 112), pastures (CLC 231), and farmland with a lot of natural plants growing on it (CLC 243).

3.3.2. Darány

In Darány, we saw a significant pattern among the six land types we looked at, and it involved forests. Mixed forest (CLC 313) made up a significantly larger share of the land around burrows with cubs than around the randomly chosen points, in several cases.

Compared with the "random 1" point, the difference was statistically significant (Table A2). The median area of mixed forest around burrows with cubs was 23.61 hectares, more than the 9.53 hectares around the random point. In the same way, we found a statistically significant difference for the "random 2" point, again with more mixed forest around burrows with cubs: the median was 23.61 hectares around the burrows and 8.49 hectares around the point (Table A4).

These results suggest that, in Darány, mixed forest (CLC 313) might be an important kind of land for burrows with cubs. For the other land types, our comparisons did not show differences that we could check with statistics. These were farmland that is not watered by irrigation (CLC 211), broad-leaved forest (CLC 311), conifer forest (CLC 312), mixed forest (CLC 313), land where woodland turns into shrubs (CLC 324), and water (CLC 512).
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

4.1. Burrows

Our study shows that counting all the burrows was a good way to study where European badgers live. It is not enough, though, for keeping an accurate watch on golden jackals and red foxes. These animals do not always use burrows to raise their cubs, and foxes can use more than one burrow at the same time to raise their young [15,16].

The number of occupied badger burrows we recorded, between 1.05 and 1.43 per 100 hectares, fits with how badgers behave. They use burrows to meet and interact with other members of their group, to breed, and to shelter through the winter [25,32,33]. This also supports what we saw about foxes and jackals: they are very flexible in how they use burrows. They can also use things on the surface, such as abandoned cellars, which can slip past a survey that looks only for burrows.

When we compare our badger burrow numbers with earlier work, our figures stand out. We found 1.05 occupied burrows per 100 hectares in Drávaszentes and 1.43 in Darány. Both are higher than the numbers from earlier studies in the Darány area [34], and both are higher than the number from an earlier study in the Drávaszentes area [35]. Our result is also higher than the estimate for eastern Hungary [36].

For red foxes, we found 0.38 occupied burrows per 100 hectares in Drávaszentes. This is similar to an earlier study at the same place [35]. In the Darány area, we found no fox burrows at all, while an earlier study there reported 0.4 burrows per 100 hectares [34]. When we compare our results with those from south-eastern Hungary, we get values between 0.23 and 0.47, which on average is roughly the same as our results [15].

For golden jackals, our result in the Darány area was similar to an earlier result from the same area, which was 0.3 burrows per 100 hectares. In eastern Hungary, two other studies of jackals found more, between 0.32 and 0.34 families per 100 hectares [15].

4.2. The Smallest Possible Number of Animals and the Number of Cubs in Litters, Seen by Wildlife Cameras

We need to be clear about one thing: our litter sizes only show the cubs that left the burrows. The cameras also have some weaknesses. They cannot see the whole burrow, only its entrance. They can only notice movement up to a certain distance, and they do not always switch on when something moves. Sometimes, when the camera does notice movement, the whole animal is not in the picture.

The badger litters we recorded had between 1.13 and 1.6 cubs. This can be compared with an earlier study in the Drávaszentes area, which found 1.29 cubs per burrow, a number that is the average of our two study areas [37]. For red foxes, our result of 2.33 cubs per litter can be compared with a study in the Drávaszentes area that found 4 cubs per litter, which is much higher.

For jackals, we did not record any cubs. This may be because jackals can move their cubs to another burrow if they feel disturbed [34].

4.3. The Kinds of Land Around Badger Burrows

Our analysis of the land around burrows showed that badgers were drawn to certain kinds of land, although which kinds differed from one study area to the other. In Drávaszentes, badger breeding burrows were linked to farmland that is not watered by irrigation (a land type in the European land-cover map called CLC 211). This link was statistically significant (p = 0.007 compared with randomly chosen points). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. For p = 0.007, that would happen less than 1 time in 1,000. This link probably reflects the "edge effect": badgers use the area between places that give them safety and farmland, where they can find food.

In Darány, on the other hand, we saw badgers drawn to mixed forests (CLC 313). This link was statistically significant too, with p = 0.032 and p = 0.016 compared with randomly chosen points. This fits with other studies, in which badgers find the soil in these areas to be stable.

The difference between the two study areas suggests that badgers are flexible in their behaviour and can choose the kinds of land that suit them best.

4.4. The Jackal Effect

We found red fox burrows and litters at only one of our two places, and none at the other, where we found jackals. This suggests that the larger golden jackal population can hold back the smaller red fox population. Badger populations, on the other hand, seem to cope well with jackals.
